17592186092083.question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^3 - x^2$ at the point $(1,0)$ is given by $y=px+q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the values of $p$ and $q.$
17592186092083.question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=x^3 - x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-{x}^{2})=3{x}^{2}-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1, 0){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=3-2=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-1$ and $q=1.$

17592186092722.question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=2{x}^{2}$ at the point $(2,8)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p+q.$
17592186092722.question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{2}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2})=4x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,8):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(2)=4(2)=8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{8}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-8 & =-\frac{1}{8}(x-2) \\ 8y-64 & =-x+2 \\ x+8y & =66.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p+q=8+66=74.$

17592186092724.question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=2{x}^{5}-2x$ at the point $(1,0)$ is given by $y=ax+b$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants. Find the value of $a+b.$
17592186092724.question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{5}-2x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{5}-2x)=10{x}^{4}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=10(1)^{4}-2=8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{8}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-\frac{1}{8}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{8}+\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a+b=-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{8}=0.$

17592186234077.question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=2{x}^{3}$ at the point $(2,16)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $q-p.$
17592186234077.question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{3}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3})=6{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,16):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{'}(2)=6(2)^{2}=24\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{'}$ is

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{24}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(16) & =-\frac{1}{24}(x-(2)) \\ 24y-384 & =-x+2 \\ x+24y & =386.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q-p=386-24=362.$

17592186238020.question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}$ at the point $(1,4)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $q-p.$
17592186238020.question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =-2{x}^{-3/2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{{1}^{3}}}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ 2y-8 & =x-1 \\ x-2y & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q-p=-7-(-2)=-5.$

17592186317214.question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt[3]{x}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{3}{2}\sqrt[3]{x}\right) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}{x}^{-2/3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $\left(\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{4}\right):$

$$
m={f}^{′}\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt[3]{{\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)}^{2}}}=2
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$

$$

17592186329814.question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x$ at the point $(1,3)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p-q.$
17592186329814.question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{-2}-x) \\  & =-8{x}^{-3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=-8(1)^{-3}-1=-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(3) & =\frac{1}{9}(x-1) \\ 9y-27 & =x-1 \\ x-9y & =-26.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p-q=-9-(-26)=17.$

f'(x)&=1 + \frac{1}{3 x^{\frac{2}{3}}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the tangent slope at the supplied abscissa:

$$
m_t=f'\left(1\right)=1 + \frac{1}{3 \left(1\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}}=\frac{4}{3}
$$

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so

$$
m_n=-\frac{1}{m_t}=-\frac{1}{\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)}=- \frac{3}{4}.
$$

Use the point in point-slope form and rearrange:

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $a=- \frac{3}{4}$ and $b=\frac{15}{4}$.

17592186091953.question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y = 2x^3 -x^2$ at the point $(1,1).$
17592186091953.question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3-x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
f'(x)  =6x^2 -2x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
m=f'(1) = 6(1)^2 - 2(1) = 4
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac 1 4.
$$

17592186233770.question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{2}+3x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
{f}^{'}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+3x)=2x+3
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(-1,-2):$

$$
m={f}^{'}(-1)=2(-1)+3=-2+3=1
$$

Therefore, the slope ${m}^{'}$ of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{'} & =-\frac{1}{m} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

17592186233924.question/worked-solution:

Therefore, the slope ${m}^{'}$ of the normal line is

17592186238012.question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}$ at the point $(1,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3/2}-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =3{x}^{1/2}-4x.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{1/2}-4(1)=-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=1.
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line  ${m}^{′}$ is

&=\frac{39}{16}.

The normal has the negative reciprocal slope:

$$

17592186091954.question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x) = 2\sqrt{x} -4x$ at the point $(1,-2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
17592186091954.question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}-4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}-4x) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

     

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1) = (1)^{-1/2} - 4 = -3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = \dfrac 1 3.
$$

The equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y+2 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{1}{3}-2 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{7}{3} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(7,0).$

17592186092507.question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2{x}^{2}+x$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
17592186092507.question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+x)=4x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=4(1)+1=5,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =-\frac{1}{5}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{1}{5}+3 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5} & =0 \\ x & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(16,0).$

17592186710708.question/problem:
Let $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}-3x+1$. Find where the normal line to the curve $y=f(x)$ at the point with $x$-coordinate $4$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$. Give exact values.
17592186710708.question/worked-solution:
First find the point on the curve:

$$
f(4)=2\sqrt{4}-3(4)+1=4-12+1=-7.
$$

Thus the normal passes through $(4,-7)$. Differentiate both variable terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=2x^{1/2}-3x+1,\\
f'(x)&=x^{-1/2}-3=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}-3.
\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent slope is

$$
f'(4)=\frac{1}{2}-3=-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

The normal slope is the negative reciprocal, so

$$
m_n=-\frac{1}{-5/2}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

Using $(4,-7)$, the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}
y+7&=\frac{2}{5}(x-4),\\
y&=\frac{2}{5}x-\frac{8}{5}-7\\
&=\frac{2}{5}x-\frac{43}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$. Solving gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
0&=\frac{2}{5}x-\frac{43}{5},\\
2x&=43,\\
x&=\frac{43}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection is $\left(\frac{43}{2},0\right)$.

17592186710717.question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $(1,1)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
17592186710717.question/worked-solution:
Differentiating gives

$$
f'(x)=2x,\qquad f'(1)=2.
$$

The tangent slope is $2$, so the normal slope is its negative reciprocal:

$$
m_n=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

The diagram shows the curve, its solid tangent, and its dashed normal at $(1,1)$.

![The parabola y equals x squared with its tangent and perpendicular normal at (1,1).](images/31/31ba09ff14e5bd485794f283c5d6a5b087b6c21fdb9242af01b75ec8e8744e0d.png)

Using point-slope form, the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-1&=-\frac{1}{2}(x-1)\\
y&=-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{3}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$. Therefore,

$$
0=-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{3}{2},\qquad x=3.
$$

The intersection is $(3,0)$.

17592186761096.question/problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=2\sqrt{x}+3x$ at the point with $x$-coordinate $1$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The intersection is $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$. Give exact values.
17592186761096.question/worked-solution:
First find the point on the curve.

$$
f(1)=2\sqrt{(1)}+3(1)=5.
$$

The normal passes through $(1,5)$.

Rewrite the radical or reciprocal using powers, then differentiate.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=2 x^{\frac{1}{2}} + 3 x, \\f'(x)&=3 + \frac{1}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}=3 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the tangent slope and take its negative reciprocal to find the normal slope.

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_t=f'(1)&=3 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1)}}=4, \\m_n=-\frac{1}{m_t}&=-\frac{1}{(4)}=- \frac{1}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use point-slope form through $(1,5)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-(5)&=- \frac{1}{4}(x-(1)), \\y&=- \frac{x}{4} + \frac{21}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
0&=- \frac{1}{4}x+\left(\frac{21}{4}\right), \\x&=21.
\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection is $(21,0)$.

17592186761097.question/problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=-4\sqrt{x}+3x+2$ at the point with $x$-coordinate $1$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The intersection is $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$. Give exact values.
17592186761097.question/worked-solution:
First find the point on the curve.

$$
f(1)=-4\sqrt{(1)}+3(1)+2=1.
$$

The normal passes through $(1,1)$.

Rewrite the radical or reciprocal using powers, then differentiate.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=- 4 x^{\frac{1}{2}} + 3 x + 2, \\f'(x)&=3 - \frac{2}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}=3 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the tangent slope and take its negative reciprocal to find the normal slope.

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_t=f'(1)&=3 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{(1)}}=1, \\m_n=-\frac{1}{m_t}&=-\frac{1}{(1)}=-1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use point-slope form through $(1,1)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-(1)&=-1(x-(1)), \\y&=- x + 2.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
0&=-1x+(2), \\x&=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection is $(2,0)$.

17592186096652.knowledge-point/title: Finding Two Scalar Factors in a Linear Combination

17592186096451.question/problem:
Consider the picture below. Given that $\mathbf{m}=\lambda\mathbf{n}+\mu\mathbf{k}$, find $\lambda$ and $\mu$.

![](images/b8/b8abf22d14f93a38c4d01f368b8171e4ccfe90086d932f5b58453baa46391405.png)
17592186096451.question/worked-solution:
![](images/76/76b9867a7c1ef484922241ebe44272f0104e406c31310bf36227a13850f50d8b.png)

In $\bigtriangleup ONM$ shown above, we have:

- $ON=2|\mathbf{n}|$;

- $\overrightarrow{ON}$ and $\mathbf{n}$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overrightarrow{ON}=2\mathbf{n}$.

Similarly:

- $NM=2|\mathbf{k}|$

- $\overrightarrow{NM}$ and $\mathbf{k}$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overrightarrow{NM}=2\mathbf{k}$.

Additionally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{m} & =\overset{\to }{ON}+\overset{\to }{NM} \\  & =2\mathbf{n}+2\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $\mathbf{m}=\lambda\mathbf{n}+\mu\mathbf{k}=2\mathbf{n}+2\mathbf{k}$. 

Since $\mathbf{n} \nparallel \mathbf{k},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{n}$ and $\mathbf{k}$, we get:

- $\lambda=2$ and $\mu=2$

![Completed vector path](images/c2/c2bcb1d71d99d24ae325386c8b99146b5854c6186b0f25ce64bfe24cf8379ef8.png)

Construct a route $O\to X\to C$ whose first segment is parallel to $\mathbf{b}$ and whose second segment is parallel to $\mathbf{a}$. The added dashed lines show this route.

A copy of $\mathbf{b}$ moves one square right and two squares up. The segment from $O$ to $X$ moves three squares right and six squares up, so $OX=3|\mathbf{b}|$ with the same direction. Thus $\overrightarrow{OX}=3\mathbf{b}$.

A copy of $\mathbf{a}$ moves two squares right and one square up. From $X$ to $C$, move four squares left and two squares down. The length is $2|\mathbf{a}|$, but the direction is opposite, so $\overrightarrow{XC}=-2\mathbf{a}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{c}&=\overrightarrow{OX}+\overrightarrow{XC}\\
&=3\mathbf{b}-2\mathbf{a}\\
&=-2\mathbf{a}+3\mathbf{b}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Because $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are not parallel, this expression is unique. Match each coefficient to its vector, rather than to the order of travel: $\lambda=-2$ and $\mu=3$.

17592186735008.question/worked-solution:
![Completed vector path](images/5d/5d7bbadbc141798871c16c1175696cf27628e2966c84d2bb2f744ff65d527c71.png)

Follow the supplied route $O\to A\to C$. On the grid, $OA$ is twice the length of $\mathbf{a}$ and points in the same direction, so $\overrightarrow{OA}=2\mathbf{a}$.

The segment from $A$ to $C$ moves six squares right and three squares down. A copy of $\mathbf{b}$ moves two squares right and one square down. Thus $AC=3|\mathbf{b}|$, with the same direction, and $\overrightarrow{AC}=3\mathbf{b}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{c}&=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AC}\\
&=2\mathbf{a}+3\mathbf{b}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are not parallel, their coefficients are unique. Matching coefficients gives $\lambda=2$ and $\mu=3$.

17592186735013.question/worked-solution:
![Completed vector path](images/be/be23bdf90ef85ad1d8b373ca25d9112b6d574c316f729c90db4269bdc3984147.png)

Draw a path $O\to X\to C$, first parallel to $\mathbf{a}$ and then parallel to $\mathbf{b}$, as shown.

From $O$ to $X$, move three squares down. The vector $\mathbf{a}$ moves two squares up, so $OX=\frac{3}{2}|\mathbf{a}|$ and the directions are opposite. Hence $\overrightarrow{OX}=-\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}$.

From $X$ to $C$, move four squares right and two squares up. This is twice the displacement of $\mathbf{b}$, in the same direction, so $\overrightarrow{XC}=2\mathbf{b}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{c}&=\overrightarrow{OX}+\overrightarrow{XC}\\
&=-\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The two reference vectors are not parallel, so matching coefficients gives $\lambda=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $\mu=2$. The negative sign records the downward part of the route; a length ratio alone does not give its sign.

17592186096452.question/problem:
Consider the following diagram, where $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a},$ $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf{b},$ and $X$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $3:1.$ Find $\overrightarrow{OX}.$

![](images/67/678ea2936b8a5b1ded74cb8a0875c629e8be0f7002c98492ebf2e8109fc603ef.png)
17592186096452.question/worked-solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overrightarrow{OX} = \overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AX}.
$$

We're told that $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a},$ so we just need to work out $\overrightarrow{AX}.$

First, from $\triangle OAB,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{AO}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b} \\  & =\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $AX:XB=3:1,$ we have

$$
\overrightarrow{AX}=\dfrac{3}{4}\overrightarrow{AB}=\dfrac{3}{4}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OX} & =\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AX} \\  & =\mathbf{a}+\frac{3}{4}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\mathbf{a}+\frac{3}{4}\mathbf{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

17592186096459.question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1 \\ y+z &=-2 \\ -x+2y+z &=-1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
17592186096459.question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1 \\ y+z &=-2 \\ z &=2,\end{aligned}\right.
$$



and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=2$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+(2) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=-4$ and $z=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(-4)+(2) &=1\,⟹\,x=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-5,$ $y=-4,$ and $z=2.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -5,-4,2 \rangle.$

17592186096937.question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
17592186096937.question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 6\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 & -20\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=19 \\ y+2z &=13 \\ z &=5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y+2(5)=13\,⟹\,y=13-10=3.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=3$ and $z=5$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(3)+2(5)=19\,⟹\,x=6.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=6,y=3$, and $z=5.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨6,3,5⟩.$

17592186266014.question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}3 & -6 & 3 & -9 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
17592186266014.question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}3 & -6 & 3 & -9 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 8\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+z &=-3 \\ y-2z &=-2 \\ z &=8,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=8$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y-2(8)=-2\,⟹\,y=-2+16=14.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=14$ and $z=8$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x-2(14)+(8)=-3\,⟹\,x=17.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=17,y=14$, and $z=8.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨17,14,8⟩.$

17592186287983.question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=6 \\ y+z &=5 \\ 2x+3y+2z &=14\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and hence solve the linear system.
17592186287983.question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 & 14\end{array}\right].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 & 14\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -3\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :=-{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=6 \\ y+z &=5 \\ z &=3,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=3$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y+(3)=5\,⟹\,y=5-3=2.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=2$ and $z=3$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(2)+(3)=6\,⟹\,x=6-5=1.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=1,y=2$ and $z=3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-3 & 3 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=1 \\ y-3z &=-9 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y-3(1)=-9\,⟹\,y=-6.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 8\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -4\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}

17592186757131.question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix is

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}3 & 0 & -6 & -9 \\ 2 & 1 & -2 & -12 \\ -2 & -2 & 1 & 17\end{array}\right].
$$

Using $R_1:=\frac{1}{3}R_1$, we obtain

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 0 & -2 & -3 \\ 2 & 1 & -2 & -12 \\ -2 & -2 & 1 & 17\end{array}\right].
$$

Using $R_2:=R_2-2R_1$, we obtain

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 0 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -6 \\ -2 & -2 & 1 & 17\end{array}\right].
$$

Using $R_3:=R_3+2R_1$, we obtain

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 0 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -6 \\ 0 & -2 & -3 & 11\end{array}\right].
$$

Using $R_3:=R_3+2R_2$, we obtain

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 0 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{array}\right].
$$

The matrix is in row echelon form: each pivot lies to the right of the pivot above it, with zeros below each pivot.

The corresponding triangular system is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2z&=-3 \\ y+2z&=-6 \\ z&=-1\end{aligned}\right..
$$

Back substitution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}z&=-1 \\ y&=-6-(2)(-1)=-4 \\ x&=-3-(0)(-4)-(-2)(-1)=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $\langle -5,-4,-1\rangle$.

17592186096673.knowledge-point/title: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Using Standard Gaussian Elimination with Row Exchanges

17592186096460.question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ x+y+2z &=-1 \\ x+2y+z &=1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
17592186096460.question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is



$$
M= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].
$$



Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get $a_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ y &=3 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$



and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z,$ and the second equation $y=3$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting these values into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+(3)+(1) &=-2\,⟹\,x=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-6,$ $y=3,$ and $z=1.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -6,3,1 \rangle.$

17592186097349.question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=8 \\ -2x+2y-3z &=-11 \\ x+z &=9.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
17592186097349.question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -11 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 9\end{array}\right].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -11 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 9\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 9\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=8 \\ y-z &=1 \\ z &=5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(5) &=1\,⟹\,y=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $y=6$ and $z=5$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(6)+2(5) &=8\,⟹\,x=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=4$, $y=6$, and $z=5.$

17592186097350.question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 & 9\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 & 9\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 & 7\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 & 7\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply the $2$nd row by $-\frac{1}{3}$ and the $3$rd row by $\frac{1}{2}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{7}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{7}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

17592186342020.question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3x+6y-3z &=18 \\ -4x+8y-3z &=2 \\ y-4z &=-3.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
17592186342020.question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-3 & 6 & -3 & 18 \\ -4 & 8 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -3\end{array}\right].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-3 & 6 & -3 & 18 \\ -4 & 8 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -3\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -2 & 1 & -6 \\ -4 & 8 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -3\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -2 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -22 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -3\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -2 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -22 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -3\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -2 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -22\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+z &=-6 \\ y-4z &=-3 \\ z &=-22,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=-22$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4(-22) &=-3\,⟹\,y=-91.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $y=-91$ and $z=-22$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2(-91)+(-22) &=-6\,⟹\,x=-166.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=-166$, $y=-91$, and $z=-22.$

$$

$$

M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & 4 & -4 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{array}\right].

$$

$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}

\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y-2z &=2 \\ y+3z &=1 \\ z &=-3,\end{aligned}\right.

$$
\begin{aligned}y+3(-3) &=1\,⟹\,y=10.\end{aligned}

Now, substituting $y=10$ and $z=-3$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2(10)-2(-3) &=2\,⟹\,x=-24.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=-24$, $y=10$, and $z=-3.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨-24,10,-3⟩.$

17592186756998.question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

The augmented matrix is

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-3 & -9 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 6 & -1 & 3 \\ -2 & -7 & 1 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize the first pivot with $R_1:=-\frac{1}{3}R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 6 & -1 & 3 \\ -2 & -7 & 1 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

$R_2:=R_2+(-2)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ -2 & -7 & 1 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

$R_3:=R_3+(2)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

The second pivot is zero, while the third row has a nonzero second entry. Exchange $R_2$ and $R_3$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize with $R_2:=-1R_2$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize with $R_3:=-1R_3$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3\end{array}\right]
$$

Thus the row echelon matrix is

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3\end{array}\right]
$$

17592186757009.question/problem:

$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system. Select the solution $(x,y,z)$.
17592186757009.question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix is

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-1 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & -3 & 3 \\ -2 & 8 & 2 & -2\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize the first pivot with $R_1:=-1R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & -3 & 3 \\ -2 & 8 & 2 & -2\end{array}\right]
$$

$R_2:=R_2+(-1)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ -2 & 8 & 2 & -2\end{array}\right]
$$

$R_3:=R_3+(2)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 & -2\end{array}\right]
$$

The second pivot is zero, while the third row has a nonzero second entry. Exchange $R_2$ and $R_3$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize with $R_2:=\frac{1}{2}R_2$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize with $R_3:=-1R_3$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3\end{array}\right]
$$

Thus the row echelon matrix is

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3\end{array}\right]
$$

Back substitute, starting with the last row:

$$
\begin{aligned}z &=-3 \\ y &=-1-(-1)(-3) \\ &=-4 \\ x &=0-(-3)(-4) \\ &\quad -(-2)(-3) \\ &=-18\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $(x,y,z)$ is

$$

Thus the row echelon matrix is

\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{array}\right]

17592186760888.question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x-3y+3z &=12 \\ -2x+2y-4z &=-12 \\ -2y-5z &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system. Select the solution $(x,y,z)$.
17592186760888.question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix is

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}3 & -3 & 3 & 12 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & -12 \\ 0 & -2 & -5 & -2\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize the first pivot with $R_1:=\frac{1}{3}R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 4 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & -12 \\ 0 & -2 & -5 & -2\end{array}\right]
$$

$R_2:=R_2+(2)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & -5 & -2\end{array}\right]
$$

The second pivot is zero, while the third row has a nonzero second entry. Exchange $R_2$ and $R_3$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -2 & -5 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & -4\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize with $R_2:=-\frac{1}{2}R_2$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{5}{2} & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & -4\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize with $R_3:=-\frac{1}{2}R_3$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{5}{2} & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{array}\right]
$$

Thus the row echelon matrix is

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{5}{2} & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{array}\right]
$$

Back substitute, starting with the last row:

$$
\begin{aligned}z &=2 \\ y &=1-\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)(2) \\ &=-4 \\ x &=4-(-1)(-4) \\ &\quad -(1)(2) \\ &=-2\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $(x,y,z)$ is

$$
\left(-2,-4,2\right)
$$

17592186760899.question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ for the variables $x,y,z$ in that order.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}3 & 6 & 0 & 15 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 & 8 \\ 0 & 3 & -4 & 2\end{array}\right]
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system. Select the solution $(x,y,z)$.
17592186760899.question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix is

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}3 & 6 & 0 & 15 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 & 8 \\ 0 & 3 & -4 & 2\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize the first pivot with $R_1:=\frac{1}{3}R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 0 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 & 8 \\ 0 & 3 & -4 & 2\end{array}\right]
$$

$R_2:=R_2+(-1)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & -4 & 2\end{array}\right]
$$

The second pivot is zero, while the third row has a nonzero second entry. Exchange $R_2$ and $R_3$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize with $R_2:=\frac{1}{3}R_2$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{4}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize with $R_3:=-\frac{1}{2}R_3$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{4}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{3}{2}\end{array}\right]
$$

Thus the row echelon matrix is

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{4}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{3}{2}\end{array}\right]
$$

Back substitute, starting with the last row:

$$
\begin{aligned}z &=-\frac{3}{2} \\ y &=\frac{2}{3}-\left(-\frac{4}{3}\right)\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) \\ &=-\frac{4}{3} \\ x &=5-(2)\left(-\frac{4}{3}\right) \\ &\quad -(0)\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{23}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $(x,y,z)$ is

$$
\left(\frac{23}{3},-\frac{4}{3},-\frac{3}{2}\right)
$$

17592186096701.knowledge-point/title: Finding a Scalar Factor in a Linear Combination

17592186096495.question/problem:
Consider the picture below.

![](images/f2/f2518c2e998e7c7f551548a4cc7283720a66428ea8fa9872494a81cc3848ba9e.png)

Given that $\mathbf{c} = \lambda  \mathbf{a} + 2 \mathbf{b}$, find $\lambda.$
17592186096495.question/worked-solution:
Recall that when two known vectors are not parallel, a linear combination of them is unique. So, once we rewrite $\mathbf c$ in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b,$ we can match coefficients to determine the unknown scalar.

To find $\lambda,$ we want to match the expression
$$
\mathbf{c} = \lambda  \mathbf{a} + 2 \mathbf{b} .
$$

We are given that one of the components is $2 \mathbf{b} .$ So, we first draw the vector $2 \mathbf{b}$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

![](images/ea/ea517ac4ca8e0bcf7ba48f23e66f100323d5485f1221219aacfbea9148f4a1af.png)

Note that in $△ O D C$, we have:

- $D C = 2 | \mathbf{a} |$

- $\overrightarrow{D C}$ and $\mathbf a$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overrightarrow{D C} = 2 \mathbf{a} .$

Additionally,
$$
\begin{array}{cc}\mathbf{c} &  = \overrightarrow{O D} + \overrightarrow{D C} \\  &  = 2 \mathbf{b} + 2 \mathbf{a} .\end{array}
$$

Consequently, $\mathbf{c} = \lambda  \mathbf{a} + 2 \mathbf{b} = 2 \mathbf{b} + 2 \mathbf{a} .$

Since $\mathbf{a} \nparallel \mathbf{b},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf a,$ we get:
$$
\lambda=2
$$

![](images/0f/0f345644213f3b78013d06f25e39df9b74ab93a0560ac7611f4b51186c47b905.png)

Given that $\mathbf{c}=\lambda\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}$, find $\lambda$.

$\lambda=$ {{field-1}}.
17592186761374.question/worked-solution:
Construct the known component $\mathbf{b}$ from $O$, ending at $B$. Count signed horizontal and vertical grid displacements:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{OB} &=1\,(0, -3)=(0, -3). \\
\overrightarrow{BC} &=(-6, 0).
\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/8a/8a4ecc321f6a818275a9281cc80a82506b9b1a3f6826cbc6dbd011b798895041.png)

Compare the remaining displacement with $\mathbf{a}$, whose grid displacement is $(-2, 0)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Horizontal scale} &=\frac{-6}{-2}=3
\end{aligned}
$$

The scale is positive, so the remaining vector has the same direction as $\mathbf{a}$. Thus $\overrightarrow{BC}=3\mathbf{a}$. By the triangle law,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{c} &=\overrightarrow{OB}+\overrightarrow{BC} \\
&=\mathbf{b}+3\mathbf{a} \\
&=3\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are not parallel, so their coefficients are unique. Matching the coefficient of $\mathbf{a}$ gives $\lambda=3$.

17592186234976.question/problem:
Consider the picture below. 

![](images/d4/d4f18c3567d0c55d3d6e002fbe2c6ac50b97b7adc14b016c8e95006de98ca15d.png)

Given that $\mathbf{c} = \lambda  \mathbf{a} - 2 \mathbf{b} ,$ find $\lambda.$
17592186234976.question/worked-solution:
To find $\lambda,$ we want to match the expression
$$
\mathbf{c} = \lambda  \mathbf{a} - 2 \mathbf{b} .
$$

We are given that one of the components is $- 2 \mathbf{b} .$ So, we first draw the vector $- 2 \mathbf{b}$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

![](images/65/65a6b5743ab9b6ef820744d0d6601b7dfd8de08a3f895661d96d2fe2cab8e0a7.png)

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $- 2 \mathbf{b} .$ Then

$$
\mathbf{c} = \overrightarrow{O P} + \overrightarrow{P C} .
$$

In $△ O P C ,$ we have:

- $O P = 2 | \mathbf{b} |$

- $\overrightarrow{OP}$ and $\mathbf b$ have opposite directions

Hence,
$$
\overrightarrow{O P} = - 2 \mathbf{b} .
$$

Similarly,

- $P C = | \mathbf{a} |$

- $\overrightarrow{P C}$ and $\mathbf a$ have opposite directions

Hence,
$$
\overrightarrow{P C} = - \mathbf{a} .
$$

Additionally,

$$
\begin{array}{cc}\mathbf{c} &  = \overrightarrow{O P} + \overrightarrow{P C} \\  &  = - 2 \mathbf{b} + ( - \mathbf{a} ) \\  &  = - \mathbf{a} - 2 \mathbf{b} .\end{array}
$$

Consequently,
$$
\mathbf{c} = \lambda  \mathbf{a} - 2 \mathbf{b} = - \mathbf{a} - 2 \mathbf{b} .
$$

Since $\mathbf{a} \nparallel \mathbf{b},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf a,$ we get

$$
\lambda=-1.
$$

17592186735154.question/worked-solution:
The known component is $-2\mathbf{b}$: reverse the direction of $\mathbf{b}$ and double its length. Starting at the common origin $O$, this takes us $4$ squares right and $4$ squares down to a point $P$.

![](images/64/646b8f1322f815e786f82eb8cfb3fa9e84a3c8d588c94910b0b702b607bfb2d8.png)

To reach the endpoint $C$ of $\mathbf{c}$ from $P$, move $6$ squares up. But $\mathbf{a}$ runs $4$ squares down. Therefore the remaining vector has the opposite direction and $\frac{6}{4}=\frac{3}{2}$ times the length of $\mathbf{a}$:
$$
\overrightarrow{PC}=-\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}.
$$
Adding the path vectors,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{c}&=\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PC}\\
&=-2\mathbf{b}-\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}\\
&=-\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}-2\mathbf{b}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Because $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are nonparallel, matching coefficients gives $\lambda=-\frac{3}{2}$. The ratio compares the remaining path with $\mathbf{a}$, not with $\mathbf{b}$.

![](images/a8/a8309dc45ac43c6642010e744de5a062d6575d48ba85bd642df39dd261f47422.png)

The vector $\mathbf{a}$ runs $4$ grid squares downward. The remaining path $\overrightarrow{PC}$ runs $8$ squares upward, so it is twice as long and points in the opposite direction:
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{c}&=\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PC}\\
&=2\mathbf{b}-2\mathbf{a}\\

The vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are nonparallel, so comparing their unique coefficients gives $\lambda=-2$. A positive $2$ would have the correct length but the wrong direction.

![](images/d2/d29b30270bcaf446c5e2c142bc081865ace2e3edec00ad9030a443ae8a071abd.png)

Following the grid direction of $\mathbf{a}$ takes $2$ steps, while the parallel path $PC$ has $7$ steps. Their length ratio is $\frac{7}{2}=\frac{7}{2}$. The remaining path points in the opposite direction to $\mathbf{a}$, so
$$
\overrightarrow{PC}=-\frac{7}{2}\mathbf{a}.
$$
Adding the path vectors gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{c}&=\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PC}\\
&=-4\mathbf{b}+\left(-\frac{7}{2}\mathbf{a}\right)\\
&=-\frac{7}{2}\mathbf{a}-4\mathbf{b}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Because $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are nonparallel, these coefficients are unique. Comparing with $\mathbf{c}=\lambda\mathbf{a}-4\mathbf{b}$ gives $\lambda=-\frac{7}{2}$. The minus sign records the reversed direction.
